name: Black rice extract

lead: Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation from the bran of dark-coloured rice, concentrated in anthocyanins. It is marketed in supplements and skincare as an antioxidant botanical, promoted for anti-aging and a brighter look.

The idea is that anthocyanin antioxidants reduce oxidative stress on skin, so fewer signs of aging show. Lab studies report it raised antioxidant enzyme activity in cells and mice and reduced inflammatory signalling in macrophage cells. Small human trials are registered on metabolic, cognitive and immune outcomes; ones on skin appearance were not found.

paras: People use it in serums and creams, or as a supplement, usually as part of a broader antioxidant or brightening routine. Results are judged over weeks to months.

No safety signals are described in the sources, and rice-based foods are widely eaten. Extract-specific safety data from human trials were not found. Anthocyanin stability and bioavailability are active research topics.

angle.text: Black rice extract is promoted in anti-aging and brightening skincare for its anthocyanin pigments, which act as antioxidants to ease oxidative stress on skin. Lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity; human skin trials were not found.

lead: Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation obtained from the bran of dark-pigmented rice (Oryza sativa), whose colour comes mainly from anthocyanins.[1][2] The grain is also called purple or forbidden rice; reference sources describe the "forbidden" label as a marketing term tied to claims of royal-only consumption.[1]

The extract is studied and sold as an antioxidant botanical. Laboratory work reports antioxidant enzyme induction and reduced inflammatory signalling in cells,[3][4] and mouse studies report effects on liver fat and, in fruit flies, lifespan.[5][6] Small human trials have been registered on metabolism, cognition, immunity and stress, but no published trial on skin or appearance was found.
infobox: Anthocyanins, mainly in the bran hull[1][2]

paras: The black trait arises from changes to the Kala4 gene, which drives anthocyanin production, and spread through natural crosses and deliberate breeding.[1] The anthocyanins concentrate in the bran hull.[1] Local names include chak-hao in Manipur and kavuni arisi in Tamil Nadu, India.[1] Chemistry papers have identified the individual anthocyanins in black rice and measured their degradation kinetics.[2]

A 2006 study reported that black rice extract inhibited LDL oxidation more than white rice extract ex vivo and increased superoxide dismutase and catalase activities in cells and in mice.[3] A 2015 study found that the extract suppressed inflammatory responses in macrophage cells through NF-kB and AP-1 pathways.[4] Mice on a high-fat diet had less liver fat after extract supplementation,[5] and fruit flies fed the extract lived longer.[6] A 2021 study tested a fermented blueberry and black rice food in a mouse model of atopic dermatitis.[7] Work on gut metabolism and prebiotic activity of its anthocyanins has been done in vitro.[8]

Research on uses is largely food science: fortifying bread with an anthocyanin-rich extract,[9] pH-sensitive packaging films containing purple and black rice extracts,[10] and microencapsulation to protect anthocyanins during digestion.[11] Black rice extract appears in cosmetic and supplement products as an antioxidant botanical, but the sources do not include cosmetic-formulation data.

No published studies on skin or appearance outcomes were found. Registered human trials on black rice or its anthocyanins include bioavailability in healthy adults (n=20),[12] cognition and BDNF in healthy subjects (n=12),[13] immune enhancement from rice bran extract (n=120),[14] perceived stress (n=80),[15] metabolic syndrome (n=101),[16] and lipid status with bilberry and black rice anthocyanins (n=55).[17] Published results for these were not among the sources.
